title: A robot starts at the top-left of an m by n grid and may move only right or down. Count how many distinct paths reach the bottom-right.
shortTitle: Unique Paths — count grid paths moving right or down

s1_definition.profdef: Grid DP where dp[i][j] is the number of paths to cell (i,j). The first row and first column are all 1 (only one way along an edge), and dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j] + dp[i][j−1]. Time O(m·n), space O(n) with a rolling row; closed form is the binomial C(m+n−2, m−1).
s1_definition.analogy: A courier at National Bank of India routes a sealed document across a grid of branch offices, only ever moving east or south. The number of ways to reach any office is the ways to reach the office to its west plus the ways to reach the office to its north.
s1_definition.oneliner: dp[i][j] = paths from above + paths from the left; edges are all 1.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Grid DP where dp[i][j] is the number of paths to cell (i,j). The first row and first column are all 1 (only one way along an edge), and dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j] + dp[i][j−1]. Time O(m·n), space O(n) with a rolling row; closed form is the binomial C(m+n−2, m−1).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A courier at National Bank of India routes a sealed document across a grid of branch offices, only ever moving east or south. The number of ways to reach any office is the ways to reach the office to its west plus the ways to reach the office to its north.

**One line to remember:** dp[i][j] = paths from above + paths from the left; edges are all 1.

sections.s2_technical:
Create a dp grid of size m by n. Fill the entire first row and first column with one, because along the top edge the robot can only keep moving right and along the left edge only down, so there is exactly one path to each edge cell. These are the base cases.

For every interior cell, the robot arrives either from directly above or directly to the left, so dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j] + dp[i][j−1]. For example: `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1];`. The answer is the bottom-right cell dp[m−1][n−1].

The time and space are O(m·n), and the space reduces to O(n) by keeping a single rolling row. A senior nuance is that there is a closed-form combinatorial answer, the binomial coefficient of m+n−2 choose m−1, because every path is a fixed arrangement of right and down moves.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a document courier moves across a grid of branch offices only east or south, and operations want to know how many distinct routes exist for capacity planning. This is exactly how Unique Paths works.

Problem 2 — Enumerating every route explicitly is exponential and infeasible on large grids. This is exactly why grid DP sums the two incoming directions.

The mini-project builds a `RoutePlanner`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input grid is three rows by seven columns.

Step 1: The entire first row and first column are set to one because there is only one straight path along each edge.

Step 2: The cell at row one column one becomes two by adding the one above and the one to the left.

Step 3: Each interior cell accumulates the sum of its top and left neighbors, so values grow across the grid.

Step 4: The sums cascade until the bottom-right cell is reached.

Step 5: The bottom-right cell holds twenty-eight, and a three-by-two grid similarly yields three.

```text
2026-10-27T02:40:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Courier Route Planner (Unique Paths)
2026-10-27T02:40:00Z [INFO] uniquePaths(3,7) = 28
2026-10-27T02:40:00Z [INFO] 3x7 grid → 28
2026-10-27T02:40:00Z [INFO] uniquePaths(3,2) = 3
2026-10-27T02:40:00Z [INFO] 3x2 grid → 3
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Unique Paths is a grid dynamic programming problem. I define dp of i and j as the number of distinct paths from the top-left to cell i, j, given that the robot moves only right or down. The base cases are the whole first row and first column, which are all ones because along an edge there is exactly one straight path.

For every interior cell the robot arrives either from directly above or directly from the left, so the number of paths to it is the sum of the paths to those two neighbors. The answer is the bottom-right cell. I can reduce the memory to a single rolling row because each row depends only on the one above it, and there is even a closed-form answer as a binomial coefficient, since every path is just a fixed arrangement of right and down moves.

In my project at National Bank of India, a document courier moved across a grid of branch offices going only east or south, and operations wanted the count of distinct routes for capacity planning. Enumerating routes explicitly is exponential, so I used this grid DP that simply sums the two incoming directions, which is linear in the number of cells.
